995.title: Traders, not armies
995.hook: Islam reached much of Southeast Asia through merchants and teachers
995.howItsDone: Muslim teaching on trade stresses honest weights, clear terms and keeping one's word, and in Southeast Asia, as elsewhere, Muslim traders may close their shops for Friday prayer and reopen afterward.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Aurangzeb and Dara Shikoh, two sons of the Taj's builder. Your line was two brothers, two paths.

A ship sits in harbor on the coast of Sumatra, waiting for the wind to turn. It could be weeks. The merchants aboard can't sail home until the monsoon shifts, so they come ashore. They rent rooms, open shops, buy pepper, sell cloth. On Friday they find a quiet place and pray together. They make friends at the market. Some marry and stay. A teacher among them starts answering questions from curious neighbors. Nobody marches in. No banners. A new part of the path begins here: East and Southeast Asia. It begins with people who came to sell things. Today: traders.
screen: `A SHIP WAITING FOR THE WIND.` → `SHOPS, FRIENDS, A FRIDAY PRAYER.` → `A NEW PART: EAST AND SOUTHEAST ASIA.`

segments.voice: Today, the call to prayer sounds across Indonesia and Malaysia. And yet, in much of the region, the faith did not arrive with a conquering army. It came along the trade routes of the Indian Ocean. Historians point to merchants from Arabia, Persia, India and China, and to Sufi teachers who traveled with them. It came slowly, port by port. Rulers of trading towns took up Islam, and their courts drew scholars. The traveler Ibn Battuta describes stopping at a port in Sumatra called Samudra and meeting its Muslim sultan, a ruler who loved to sit with scholars and debate. Why would merchants make good messengers? Partly because Islam has a lot to say about trade. Tradition remembers the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, as a merchant before his call. The Qur'an tells believers not to consume one another's wealth wrongly, but to trade by mutual consent. And of the Friday prayer it says, in Pickthall's translation: "And when the prayer is ended, then disperse in the land and seek of Allah's bounty." Prayer, then the market. A saying of the Prophet in Sahih al-Bukhari says that when buyer and seller are truthful and make things clear, their deal is blessed, and when they hide and lie, the blessing is wiped out. A merchant who weighs fairly, keeps his word, and closes the shop for prayer is a kind of sermon nobody has to preach. As the story is often told, neighbors watched how these traders lived before they listened to what they believed. Merchants carried it.

segments.voice: Think about the exchanges in your week: what you buy, sell, get paid for or promise, a job, a favor, a bill you split. Is there one where you've been a little less than clear? Don't scold yourself; just name it, and picture what clear would look like, and if you pray, ask for honest hands.

996.title: Malacca on the straits
996.hook: a sultanate on the straits, a hub of trade and learning
996.howItsDone: In Malaysia, Malacca's history as a Muslim sultanate is taught as part of the country's story, and Malay is still written in Jawi script in some religious and traditional settings.

segments.voice: Yesterday: traders, carrying Islam across the sea port by port. Your line was merchants carried it.

A prince on the run is resting under a tree by a river mouth. His hunting dogs are out in the brush. Suddenly they corner a mouse-deer, a tiny, delicate animal. And the mouse-deer turns around and kicks one of the dogs straight into the river. The prince laughs, amazed. A place where even the smallest creature stands its ground, he says, is a good place for a city. He asks the name of the tree he's sitting under. It's a melaka tree. That's how the Malay Annals tell the city's beginning. Today: Malacca on the straits.
screen: `A PRINCE UNDER A TREE.` → `A MOUSE-DEER KICKS A DOG.` → `A CITY NAMED FOR THE TREE.`

segments.voice: Malacca sat on a narrow sea lane between the Malay Peninsula and Sumatra: the Straits of Malacca. And it had something no fort can build: the winds. The monsoon blows one way for part of the year and the other way for the rest. Ships from India and Arabia came in on one wind, ships from China on the other, and both had to wait in port until the wind turned back. So Malacca became the place to wait, and to trade. Its rulers took up Islam, and took the Arabic title sultan. The Malay Annals tell this as a story too: the king dreams that the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, teaches him the declaration of faith, and the next day a ship arrives carrying a scholar who leads the prayer, just as the dream foretold. Whatever happened, Malacca became a center not only of trade but of learning. Scholars and Sufi teachers came. The Malay language became a language of Islamic teaching and of commerce across the islands, written in an Arabic-based script called Jawi. Merchants from many lands lived in their own quarters, with their own heads, and dealt in pepper, cloth, spices, porcelain and gold. The Qur'an speaks of ships at sea as a sign: it says God made the sea of service, so ships could run on it and people could seek of His bounty, and give thanks. Later, Portuguese ships came and took the city, and the sultans moved on. But the language, the script and the faith had already traveled. The port of the straits.

997.title: The nine saints of Java
997.hook: nine saints remembered for teaching Islam through local arts and music
997.howItsDone: Javanese Muslims visit the graves of the Wali Songo as places of remembrance and prayer, and songs attributed to them, such as Tombo Ati, are still sung in homes, schools and mosques.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Jawi, and Malacca, the port of the straits, where ships waited for the wind and traders, teachers and stories passed through.

Night on the island of Java. A white screen is stretched tight, a lamp burns behind it, and flat leather puppets throw long shadows across the cloth. An orchestra of bronze gongs and metal keys, the gamelan, rings and shimmers. A single puppeteer gives voice to kings, clowns and heroes until nearly dawn. So what would a teacher of a new faith do with a night like that? Ban it? Ignore it? Or step behind the screen and pick up a puppet? Javanese tradition has an answer, and it comes with nine names. Today: the Wali Songo.
screen: `A SCREEN, A LAMP, A PUPPET.` → `THE GAMELAN RINGS.` → `WHAT DOES A TEACHER DO?`

segments.voice: Wali Songo is usually rendered the nine saints. Wali is the Arabic word for a friend or close one of God; songo is the Javanese word for nine. Javanese tradition remembers these nine teachers as the ones who brought Islam deep into the island, and their stories share one thread: they spoke the island's own language. The best-known belongs to Sunan Kalijaga. Tradition says he took up the wayang, the shadow puppet play, and told its old tales so they carried new meaning, with the gamelan still ringing behind him. Sunan Bonang is remembered as a musician. A Javanese song called Tombo Ati, medicine for the heart, is attributed to him, and it's still sung today. Its verses name remedies for a troubled heart: reading the Qur'an and thinking on its meaning, prayer in the night, sitting with good people, fasting, and the long remembrance of God. A teaching set to a tune people could carry home. Historians still argue over how much of these stories is history and how much is loving memory. Pilgrims still visit their graves. The Qur'an says: "Call unto the way of thy Lord with wisdom and fair exhortation." As Java remembers them, the nine saints carried that wisdom in a tune the listener already knew. Not a new instrument. A new song on the old one. They taught with music.

998.title: Indonesia, the largest
998.hook: the country with the most Muslims in the world
998.howItsDone: Indonesian Muslims pray in Arabic, often hear the Friday sermon in Indonesian or a local language, and students may study in pesantren or schools run by movements such as Nahdlatul Ulama and Muhammadiyah.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Wali Songo, the nine saints of Java, who taught with music.

Quick question. Where do the most Muslims on earth live? Not, by the usual count, in the lands of Arabic street signs. Go far to the east, across an ocean, to a country of islands, volcanoes and rice terraces, where the street signs are in the Latin alphabet and the call to prayer drifts over palm trees and motorbikes. Java, where the nine saints taught, is one of its islands. Today: Indonesia.
screen: `WHERE DO THE MOST MUSLIMS LIVE?` → `NOT WHERE THE FIRST GUESS LANDS.` → `ISLANDS, VOLCANOES, RICE.`

segments.voice: Indonesia is usually counted as the country with the largest Muslim population in the world. And inside that line is a surprise: the faith that arrived with traders and teachers didn't erase the islands' languages. It learned them. Indonesians speak many languages at home and share one national language, Bahasa Indonesia, written in Latin letters. The prayers are in Arabic, the sermons often in Indonesian, and the songs may be in Javanese or Sundanese or another island tongue. The Qur'an has a line for that: "And of His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the difference of your languages and colours." In that verse, differences of language aren't a problem to be solved. They're signs. Indonesia also holds its Muslims alongside neighbors of other faiths: Christians, Hindus in Bali, Buddhists, Confucians. Its national motto is Old Javanese, Bhinneka Tunggal Ika, usually rendered unity in diversity. Among Muslims there, two well-known movements stand out. Nahdlatul Ulama tends to keep the older customs: the pesantren, the village boarding school, and visiting the graves of saints. Muhammadiyah, more of a reform movement, runs schools and hospitals and prefers a plainer practice. They differ, they argue, and both are deeply Indonesian. So the number is only the doorway. Inside is a faith that speaks with many island accents.

999.title: Brunei and the Philippines
999.hook: Muslim sultanates of Borneo and Mindanao
999.howItsDone: In Brunei, Islam shapes public life and Malay is written in both Latin letters and Jawi; Muslims of the southern Philippines keep their own languages, sung epics such as the Darangen, and traditions from the old sultanates.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Indonesia, usually counted the largest Muslim country, where one faith speaks in many island languages.

A street sign in Brunei, on the island of Borneo. The road's name is written twice: once in Latin letters, the way Malay is usually written today, and once above it in flowing Arabic letters. Same words, same language, two alphabets. That second script, Jawi, is Malay written in the letters of the Qur'an, a small daily clue to a bigger story. North and east of Borneo, across the sea, on the southern islands of the Philippines, there are clues like it. Today: Brunei and the Philippines.
screen: `A STREET SIGN IN BRUNEI.` → `ONE NAME, TWO ALPHABETS.` → `JAWI: MALAY IN ARABIC LETTERS.`

segments.voice: The trade winds that carried merchants to Malacca also carried them along the coasts of Borneo and up into the southern Philippine islands. Where trading towns took up Islam, local rulers often took a new title: sultan. On Borneo, the Sultanate of Brunei grew into a sea power along the coast. It's still ruled by a sultan today, with Islam at the heart of public life and Jawi on its signs. Further north, on the islands of Sulu and Mindanao, the Sultanates of Sulu and Maguindanao rose and ruled the seas and rivers around them. Their Muslim peoples, the Tausug, the Maguindanao, the Maranao and others, are often called together the Moro. When Spain later took the northern islands, the southern sultanates resisted, and that history of struggle over land and self-rule runs long and hard, into modern times. Today much of the Muslim south forms the Bangsamoro autonomous region, within the Philippines. And there are stories. Around Lake Lanao, the Maranao keep the Darangen, a long epic sung by performers, full of heroes, journeys, love and the old kingdom of Bembaran, sung at weddings and gatherings to hold up a people's memory of who they are. The Qur'an says: "O mankind! Lo! We have created you male and female, and have made you nations and tribes that ye may know one another." Sultans, seas, an epic by a lake. The sultanates of the islands.

1000.title: The Hui of China
1000.hook: Chinese-speaking Muslims whose ancestors came as traders and settled
1000.howItsDone: Hui Muslims pray in mosques called qingzhen si, keep halal kitchens marked qingzhen, and speak Chinese as their own language; Hui cooking, such as beef noodles and lamb dishes, is known across China.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Moro and the sultanates of the islands, Brunei's Jawi signs, and the Darangen sung by Lake Lanao.

A noodle shop on a busy street in a Chinese city. Steam on the windows. A cook slaps a rope of dough against the counter, stretches it, folds it, stretches it again, until it falls into the pot as a tangle of thin strands. The broth is beef. There's no pork anywhere in the kitchen. Above the door, two Chinese characters: qingzhen. The cook wears a small white cap. Everything here is Chinese, down to the chopsticks, and everything here is halal. Today: the Hui of China.
screen: `A NOODLE SHOP, STEAM ON THE GLASS.` → `NO PORK IN THE KITCHEN.` → `QINGZHEN ABOVE THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: The Hui are Muslims who speak Chinese as their own language. Their story, as Hui families and historians tell it, begins with traders: Arab and Persian merchants who came to China's ports by sea and its cities by the Silk Road, and later others from Central Asia. Some stayed. They married local women, raised children who spoke Chinese, and kept the prayer. Over generations the newcomers became neighbors, and the neighbors became a people. They don't have a separate homeland language or a far-off country to point to. They're Chinese all the way through, and Muslim all the way through. Their word for halal carries the same double belonging. Qingzhen is usually rendered pure and true. It's written over restaurants and butcher shops, and it names a mosque too: a qingzhen si, a temple of the pure and true. Hui scholars went further. Writers such as Wang Daiyu and Liu Zhi explained Islam in classical Chinese, using the vocabulary of Confucian learning, so Chinese readers could meet the faith in their own philosophy. People often quote a saying about this land, attributed to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him: seek knowledge even as far as China. Hadith scholars have judged it weak, so it can't be leaned on as his words. But the Hui never needed it to belong. Their ancestors came, settled, and stayed. Chinese and Muslim.

Think about where you could find it, or how you might make a simple version. If you're Muslim, you might begin it with bismillah; if not, just notice the hands that make it.
Hui. Chinese-speaking Muslims whose ancestors came as traders, settled, and became a people of their own in China. Today's word.
Your line: chinese and muslim. Both, all the way through. A thousand days, and thank you for every one.

1001.title: Xi'an's Great Mosque
1001.hook: a mosque built like a Chinese temple, with a pagoda minaret
1001.howItsDone: The Great Mosque of Xi'an is still a working mosque for the Hui community of the city's old Muslim quarter, who pray there facing west toward Mecca; visitors walk through its courtyards outside prayer times.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Hui, Chinese and Muslim, and the word qingzhen, pure and true.

Step off a crowded lane in the old city of Xi'an, past stalls selling dates and lamb skewers, through a gate with a curved tiled roof. Inside: a garden courtyard, stone tablets carved with Chinese characters, a carved wooden archway, painted and lacquered. Then another courtyard, and another, each quieter than the last. In the middle stands a tiered tower with upturned eaves like a pagoda. Everything says Chinese temple. Then, at the far end, people line up shoulder to shoulder, and someone calls Allahu akbar. Today: Xi'an's Great Mosque.
screen: `A GATE WITH A CURVED TILED ROOF.` → `COURTYARD AFTER COURTYARD.` → `A TOWER LIKE A PAGODA.`

segments.voice: Tradition says the Great Mosque of Xi'an goes back to the Tang dynasty; much of what stands today was built in later centuries. Either way, the builders made a choice. They didn't import a domed mosque from somewhere else. They built in the language of the place: courtyards one after another, wooden halls on stone platforms, roofs of glazed tile. The tower in the courtyard serves as the minaret, but it looks like a pagoda pavilion, and its Chinese name speaks of examining the heart. In the prayer hall, Arabic verses and Chinese decoration sit side by side, sometimes so blended that the Arabic letters curl like Chinese brushwork. One thing doesn't change with the clothes. The Qur'an tells the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him: "So turn thy face toward the Inviolable Place of Worship." In Xi'an that means west, toward Mecca, so the long line of courtyards runs east to west, and the prayer hall sits at the western end. Chinese walls, Chinese roofs, a Chinese garden, and a direction that points across the continent to the Ka'ba. Look back at this week: traders, not armies; the port of the straits; nine saints who taught with music; one faith in many island languages; the sultanates of the islands; the Hui. This building holds the whole week in wood and tile. A mosque in Chinese dress.
screen: `BUILT IN THE LANGUAGE OF THE PLACE.` · `A PAGODA THAT SERVES AS A MINARET.` · `ARABIC AND CHINESE SIDE BY SIDE.` · `ALL OF IT FACING WEST, TOWARD MECCA.` · then, large: `A MOSQUE IN CHINESE DRESS.`

segments.voice: Walk slowly, in your mind, through the courtyards as they were described: the gate, the garden, the stone tablets, the tower, the long hall at the western end. Notice which way you're walking, and look for one place where an Arabic word and a Chinese roof meet. If you pray, you can turn toward your own qibla.
Xi'an. The Chinese city whose Great Mosque is built like a Chinese temple, with a pagoda tower for a minaret and a prayer hall facing west. Today's word.
Your line: a mosque in chinese dress. The clothes change; the direction doesn't. That's the week.
